title: ❤️ Human Values Quest
theme: Navigate ethical dilemmas and build strong character
description: Life presents tough choices! You have 500 Mento Coins representing your personal resources (time, energy, influence). Navigate real ethical dilemmas testing honesty, compassion, courage, responsibility, respect, and integrity. Every choice shapes who you become. There are no perfect answers - only the person you choose to be.

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each ethical dilemma scenario carefully -- there are no easy answers
Choose from the available options based on your values and judgment
Watch how your choice affects traits like Honesty, Compassion, Courage, and Inner Peace
Manage your Personal Resources (Mento Coins) -- some choices cost more than others
Reflect on the outcome and feedback after each round to grow your character
tips: There are no 'wrong' answers -- the game rewards thoughtful decision-making over any single strategy
Balance short-term costs against long-term character growth
Pay attention to how different values can sometimes conflict with each other

learning_objectives: Navigate ethical dilemmas involving honesty, loyalty, courage, and compassion to understand how personal values shape decision-making
Recognize the difference between enabling and empowering others, and learn to set healthy boundaries while remaining compassionate
Develop moral courage to stand up against injustice, peer pressure, and authority figures when the situation demands it
Understand how values can conflict with each other, such as honesty versus loyalty, and practice finding creative ethical solutions
Reflect on how choices affect inner peace, self-respect, and relationships, building awareness that character is formed through everyday decisions

rounds.title: Round 1: The Honesty Test
rounds.story:
Walking home from school, you find a wallet on the sidewalk.

Inside:
• 200 Mento Coins in cash
• Driver's license with name and address
• Credit cards
• Photos of family

Nobody saw you pick it up. You're alone. No cameras nearby.

You need money - your birthday gift for mom is 150 MC short. This would solve that problem instantly.

But this money belongs to someone. The ID shows their address is 15 minutes away.

Your self-respect: {{self_respect}}%
Your honesty: {{honesty}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Test your honesty when nobody is watching
rounds.setting: Walking home - alone with your conscience

choices.label: Return Immediately to Address
choices.description: Walk 15 minutes to return wallet immediately. You'll be late for dinner and miss solving your money problem, but it's the right thing. Character is who you are when nobody's watching.
choices.feedback: You walk to the address. Woman answers door - she's been crying, wallet had her late husband's photo. She's so grateful she offers reward. You decline. The look of relief on her face is worth more than money. You feel proud.

choices.label: Turn In to Police Station
choices.description: Take wallet to police lost and found. Let authorities handle it. Less personal but still honest. Fulfill duty without going extra mile.
choices.feedback: You drop wallet at police station. Officer thanks you and takes report. Job done. You followed rules and did right thing. Not personal connection, but wallet will be returned. You did your civic duty.

choices.label: Keep Cash, Return Wallet Anonymously
choices.description: Take the 200 MC cash but mail wallet back with credit cards and ID. Rationalization: They have money, you need it, at least they get important stuff back. But is partial honesty real honesty?
choices.feedback: You take cash and mail wallet. Problem solved! But that night, lying in bed, it doesn't feel right. You rationalized theft. The inner voice asking 'what if that was your wallet?' won't quiet down. You have money but lost something else.

choices.label: Keep Wallet and Contents
choices.description: Finders keepers. They should have been more careful. You need this money more than they do. Besides, nobody knows. What they don't know won't hurt them, right?
choices.feedback: You keep it all. Next day, you see 'LOST WALLET' posters all over school - it was a student's parent. Reward offered. They're desperate. You avoid eye contact. The money in your pocket feels heavier each day. You got away with it, but did you really?

rounds.image_prompt: a quiet suburban sidewalk lined with trees and colorful houses, a brown leather wallet lying open on the pavement, sunlight filtering through leaves, a sense of temptation in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Loyalty Test
rounds.story:
Your best friend Maya asks you to lie for her.

Situation:
• Maya's parents think she's sleeping at your house Friday
• She's actually going to party with older kids
• She's asked you to cover: 'If they call, say I'm here'
• You're worried - these kids drink, drive recklessly
• But Maya is your BEST friend since kindergarten
• She says: 'Real friends have each other's backs'

Your honesty: {{honesty}}%
Your relationships: {{relationships}}%
Your integrity: {{integrity}}%

Lying is wrong. But abandoning friends is wrong too. What do you do?
rounds.goal: Navigate conflict between honesty and loyalty
rounds.setting: Friday afternoon - Maya waiting for your answer

choices.label: Refuse to Lie - Explain Why
choices.description: Tell Maya you love her but can't lie for her. You're worried about her safety. Real friendship means being honest, even when it's hard. Offer alternatives: going with her, talking to parents together.
choices.feedback: Maya is angry: 'I thought you were my friend!' She goes anyway, ignoring you. Rough weekend. But Monday, she admits party was bad scene. Next month she thanks you: 'You were being a real friend.' True friendship includes hard conversations.

choices.label: Agree to Cover for Her
choices.description: Say you'll lie if parents call. She's going anyway - might as well help. Real friends support each other, right? Besides, she'd do same for you. Keep the friendship smooth.
choices.feedback: Her parents DO call. You lie convincingly. Maya has 'great time.' But you feel sick. What if something happened? You're complicit now. A week later she asks you to lie again. Where's the line? You've crossed into territory that doesn't feel right.

choices.label: Talk to Her Parents Yourself
choices.description: You're scared for Maya's safety. Tell her parents what's happening. She'll hate you. She'll call you a traitor. But better alive and angry than... you don't want to think about alternatives.
choices.feedback: You tell her parents. Maya is grounded and FURIOUS: 'You're dead to me!' She won't speak to you for months. It's painful. But when senior dies in drunk driving accident later that year, Maya quietly texts: 'Thank you. I could have been there.' Forgiveness takes time.

choices.label: Offer to Go With Her
choices.description: Don't lie, but don't abandon her either. Say you'll go to the party with her. Keep her safe. Tell your parents the truth, ask if you can both go. Honest solution that maintains friendship.
choices.feedback: Creative compromise! Your parents surprisingly agree (with curfew). You go together. Party is sketchy - you both leave early. Maya admits she didn't really want to go alone anyway. You found third way: honesty AND friendship. Solomon would be proud.

rounds.image_prompt: a cozy bedroom with a colorful bedspread, a phone on a nightstand lighting up with an incoming call, a worried expression on a character's face, evening light filtering through curtains
rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 3: Standing Up Against Injustice
rounds.story:
Classroom scenario that tests your courage.

What Happened:
• Teacher asks 'Who drew inappropriate picture on board?'
• Quiet kid Sarah getting blamed (she didn't do it)
• You saw popular kid Jake do it before class
• Jake is star athlete, teacher's favorite
• Sarah is already struggling, this could get her suspended
• Your classmates are silent - everyone protecting Jake
• Teacher is about to write Sarah up

Your courage: {{courage}}%
Your integrity: {{integrity}}%
Your self_respect: {{self_respect}}%

Time is running out. Sarah is crying. What do you do?
rounds.goal: Test moral courage against social pressure

choices.label: Speak Up - Tell Truth Publicly
choices.description: Raise your hand and tell truth in front of whole class. Jake did it, not Sarah. Expect backlash from Jake and his friends. You'll be called a snitch. But injustice is happening right now.
choices.feedback: Hand up. You tell the truth. Room goes silent. Jake glares. Teacher thanks you. Sarah is cleared. Hallway later, Jake's friends call you snitch. But Sarah hugs you crying. Mr. Jackson pulls you aside: 'That took real courage.' You stood up. It cost something. Worth it.

choices.label: Tell Teacher Privately After Class
choices.description: Wait until class ends. Tell teacher privately what you saw. Avoid public confrontation. Sarah might still get written up today but you'll correct it later. Less dramatic, less risk.
choices.feedback: You wait. Sarah gets written up (you feel guilty). After class you tell teacher. She clears Sarah next day. Sarah asks why you didn't speak up sooner - that write-up hurt. You did right thing but timing matters. Courage delayed is courage diminished.

choices.label: Stay Silent - Don't Get Involved
choices.description: Not your problem. Getting involved makes you a target. Besides, Sarah will be fine - it's just one write-up. Don't risk your social standing for someone you barely know. Self-preservation.
choices.feedback: You stay silent. Sarah suspended 3 days. You see her mom crying in office. That night you can't sleep. You keep thinking 'I could have helped.' Week later, Mr. Jackson talks about Holocaust: 'All it takes for evil to triumph is for good people to do nothing.' You feel sick. You were that person.

choices.label: Leave Anonymous Note for Teacher
choices.description: Write note explaining what happened, slip it under teacher's door. Truth gets revealed, nobody knows it was you. Compromise between courage and caution. Is anonymous truth still courage?
choices.feedback: Anonymous note left. Teacher clears Sarah next day. Justice served. But you wrestle with question: If doing right thing, why hide? Courage means standing behind your words. You helped Sarah but didn't grow as much as you could have. Half-courage.

rounds.image_prompt: a bright, colorful classroom filled with desks and a chalkboard, students sitting silently, a distressed girl in tears at the front, a teacher poised with a clipboard, tension in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: How might your team react to this decision? What about your customers?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 4: Compassion Meets Boundaries
rounds.story:
Classmate Alex constantly asks to copy your homework.

Context:
• Alex has difficult home life - parents fighting, no support
• You empathize - life is hard for Alex
• But it's every day now
• Your grades might suffer if you keep helping this way
• Alex says: 'You're my only friend who helps'
• Teacher starting to notice similar answers
• You worked hard on this homework

Your compassion: {{compassion}}%
Your responsibility: {{responsibility}}%
Your self_respect: {{self_respect}}%

Compassion is good. But is this really helping? Where's the boundary?

choices.label: Refuse Copying, Offer Real Help
choices.description: Say no to copying but offer to study together after school. Teach Alex how to do it rather than doing it for them. Real compassion means helping people grow, not enabling dependence.
choices.feedback: You explain: 'I care about you, but copying doesn't help you learn. Let's study together.' Alex initially upset. But you spend hour helping after school. Alex starts understanding material. Grades slowly improve. True compassion empowers, doesn't enable. This is love.

choices.label: Keep Sharing Homework
choices.description: Alex needs help. You have privilege of supportive home. It's just homework. Share generously. Besides, making Alex feel bad won't help their situation. Be the friend they need.
choices.feedback: You keep sharing. Alex never learns to do own work. Teacher catches similar answers - you BOTH get zeros for cheating. Alex is angry at YOU for getting caught. Your grades drop. Parents disappointed. You learned: Enabling isn't compassion. It hurts everyone.

choices.label: Connect Alex with School Resources
choices.description: This is bigger than homework. Alex needs real help - counselor, tutoring, maybe even social services. Guide Alex to proper resources. You're not therapist or parent - know your limits.
choices.feedback: You suggest meeting counselor together. Alex reluctant but goes. Counselor connects Alex with tutoring, talks about home situation, provides real support. Three months later, Alex thanks you: 'You actually helped instead of just pitying me.' Sometimes love means connecting people to real help.

choices.label: Refuse and Distance Yourself
choices.description: You're being used. Alex is taking advantage of your kindness. Enough. Say no and reduce contact. You have your own life and problems. Protect yourself first.
choices.feedback: You cut Alex off. Alex stops asking - stops talking to you entirely. You feel relieved initially. But guilt creeps in. Was there no middle ground? Boundaries are healthy, but complete rejection isn't compassion. You protected yourself but lost opportunity to genuinely help. Gray area.

rounds.image_prompt: a cozy classroom filled with colorful posters, students at their desks, one looking worried while glancing at a friend struggling with homework in the corner, soft afternoon light filtering through the windows
rounds.coaching_moment: Look at your current resource levels — which constraint are you trying to address?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you make this choice? What values or priorities guided you?

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 5: Honesty vs. Kindness
rounds.story:
Your best friend Ananya has been practicing for weeks for the school talent show. She's singing a song she wrote herself. She asks you honestly: "How do I sound?"

The truth? Her singing is off-key and the lyrics need work. But she's poured her heart into this and the show is tomorrow. There's no time to improve significantly.

Your honesty: {{honesty}}%
Your compassion: {{compassion}}%
Your relationships: {{relationships}}%

Several other friends are watching, waiting to hear your response. Ananya trusts your opinion more than anyone else's.

What do you say?
rounds.goal: Navigate the tension between honesty and kindness

choices.label: Honest but Gentle
choices.description: Tell her the truth gently: the lyrics are beautiful but a few notes need adjustment. Offer to help her practice the tricky parts tonight. Be honest AND supportive.
choices.feedback: Ananya was nervous hearing the truth, but your offer to help meant everything. You stayed up late practicing together. At the show, she wasn't perfect — but she was better. She thanked you for being the one friend who cares enough to be honest. That's real friendship.

choices.label: Tell the Blunt Truth
choices.description: Be completely honest: the singing needs a lot of work and performing tomorrow could be embarrassing. Suggest she switch to reading her lyrics as a poem instead.
choices.feedback: Ananya was crushed. She didn't perform at all. Other friends called you harsh. Honesty without kindness is cruelty. The truth matters, but so does how and when you deliver it. Timing and tone are part of being truthful.

choices.label: Tell Her She Sounds Great
choices.description: She needs confidence, not criticism. Tell her she sounds amazing and cheer her on. Protect her feelings — that's what friends do. The show is just for fun anyway.
choices.feedback: Ananya performed with confidence — but struggled on stage. She saw the audience's awkward faces. Later she asked, 'Why didn't you tell me?' She felt betrayed by your false encouragement. Kindness without honesty isn't really kind — it's just comfortable.

choices.label: Focus on Her Strengths Instead
choices.description: Don't comment on the singing directly. Instead, highlight what IS strong — her stage presence, her original lyrics, her courage to perform. Suggest she lean into those strengths.
choices.feedback: Ananya adjusted her performance to showcase her lyrics and storytelling. The audience loved her personality even if the notes weren't perfect. You found a way to be supportive without lying. Sometimes wisdom means changing the question, not just answering it.

rounds.coaching_moment: The highest form of honesty includes kindness. The highest form of kindness includes honesty.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is it possible to be both completely honest and completely kind? When they conflict, which matters more?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Fairness Dilemma
rounds.story:
You're captain of the school quiz team. There are 5 spots for the inter-school competition but 6 deserving members.

The sixth member is Ravi — he's been on the team for 3 years and is a senior. This is his last chance to compete. But the newest member, Aisha, scored higher than Ravi in the selection test.

Ravi has seniority. Aisha has merit. Both have valid claims.

Your self-respect: {{self_respect}}%
Your relationships: {{relationships}}%
Your reputation: {{reputation}}%

The whole team is watching your decision. Whatever you choose sets a precedent for future selections.

How do you decide?

choices.label: Choose Based on Merit
choices.description: Select the top 5 scorers, including Aisha. The rules were clear — highest scores make the team. Ravi had a fair chance and Aisha earned her spot. Fairness means following the criteria everyone agreed to.
choices.feedback: Aisha was thrilled. Ravi was devastated but said quietly, 'At least I know the selection was fair.' Some seniors were upset, but underclassmen felt inspired — merit matters here. You established a culture of earned achievement.

choices.label: Honor Seniority
choices.description: Give Ravi the spot — he's earned it through years of dedication. Aisha is talented and will have more chances. Experience and loyalty should count for something beyond just test scores.
choices.feedback: Ravi was deeply grateful, but Aisha felt the system was rigged. Two junior members questioned why they should try hard if seniority always wins. When we reward loyalty over performance, we risk losing our best talent.

choices.label: Find a Creative Alternative
choices.description: Appeal to the competition organizers for a 6th spot, or create an alternate role for the 6th person (research support/substitute). Try to include everyone without compromising the merit system.
choices.feedback: You got Ravi approved as team alternate — he travels with the team, subs if needed, and helps with strategy. Everyone felt valued. Sometimes the best solution isn't choosing between two options — it's creating a third one.

choices.label: Let the Team Vote
choices.description: Present both cases to the team and let them vote anonymously. The team should decide who represents them. Democratic decision-making shares the burden.
choices.feedback: The vote was split 3-3 with you as tiebreaker. You ended up deciding anyway, but now with added pressure and public scrutiny. Sometimes democratic processes work, but leaders are chosen to make hard calls — not avoid them.

rounds.coaching_moment: Fairness doesn't always mean treating everyone the same — it means giving everyone what they deserve based on clear, consistent principles.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What does fairness mean to you — equal treatment, earned reward, or something else entirely?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 7: Taking Responsibility
rounds.story:
You were supposed to submit a group project for your team of 4. The deadline was today at 5 PM. You completely forgot.

The teacher gives a zero to the entire group. Your teammates are furious — they did their parts on time and trusted you to submit.

Your self-respect: {{self_respect}}%
Your inner peace: {{inner_peace}}%
Your responsibility: {{responsibility}}%

One teammate, Dev, says: 'This is going to drop my grade to a B. I needed that A for my scholarship application.'

The weight of your mistake hits hard. How do you respond?
rounds.goal: Learn to take responsibility for mistakes and make amends
rounds.setting: School corridor — right after results are announced

choices.label: Own It Completely
choices.description: Apologize sincerely to each teammate individually. Go to the teacher, explain it was entirely your fault, and ask if your teammates can resubmit their portions for partial credit. Offer to do extra work to make up for it.
choices.feedback: The teacher appreciated your honesty and allowed partial credit for teammates. Dev's grade was saved. Your teammates were still disappointed but respected your accountability. Owning mistakes fully is one of the bravest things you can do.

choices.label: Explain with Excuses
choices.description: You were overwhelmed with other commitments. Explain to everyone that you had too much on your plate — it wasn't intentional. Ask for understanding. Everyone makes mistakes.
choices.feedback: Your teammates weren't impressed. 'We were all busy too,' Dev said. Excuses shift blame without solving the problem. Everyone makes mistakes — but not everyone makes excuses. The difference matters.

choices.label: Blame the Submission System
choices.description: Say the online portal was down and you couldn't submit. Technology fails all the time — it's plausible. This protects you from blame and might get the whole group an extension.
choices.feedback: The teacher checked the portal logs — it was working fine. Now you're caught in a lie on top of the original mistake. Your teammates are more angry about the lying than the missed deadline. One mistake can be forgiven; dishonesty destroys trust.

choices.label: Apologize and Create Prevention Plan
choices.description: Apologize sincerely AND present a concrete plan: set up shared calendar reminders, create a backup submission person, offer to be the last-resort checker on future projects. Turn this failure into a system improvement.
choices.feedback: Your teammates were impressed. Not only did you own the mistake, you made sure it could never happen again. The shared calendar system was adopted by other groups too. True responsibility isn't just saying sorry — it's making sure it doesn't happen again.

rounds.coaching_moment: Mistakes don't define you — how you respond to them does. Take responsibility, make amends, and build systems to do better.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you make a mistake, what's your first instinct — defend, deny, or own it? Why?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 8: Compassion in Action
rounds.story:
There's a new student at school — Vikram. He recently moved from a small village and is struggling to fit in. His clothes are worn, his Hindi accent is different, and some students have been mocking him behind his back.

At lunch, you see Vikram sitting alone. Your friend group is at the popular table. You notice two classmates mimicking his accent and laughing.

Your compassion: {{compassion}}%
Your courage: {{courage}}%
Your reputation: {{reputation}}%

Vikram catches your eye. He looks like he's about to cry.

No teacher is watching. Nobody will judge you if you do nothing. But you'll know.

What do you do?

choices.label: Stand Up and Include Him
choices.description: Walk over to the mockers first. Firmly tell them to stop. Then invite Vikram to join your table. Introduce him to your friends. Make space at the popular table for someone who needs it.
choices.feedback: Vikram lit up. The mockers were embarrassed and stopped. Your friends were surprised but followed your lead. Over the next weeks, Vikram became a valued friend — turns out he's an amazing storyteller. Your one brave moment changed someone's entire school experience.

choices.label: Quietly Sit with Vikram
choices.description: Don't make a scene. Simply take your tray and sit with Vikram. Talk to him normally. Your presence speaks louder than words. Others might follow, or they might not — but Vikram won't be alone.
choices.feedback: Vikram was surprised and grateful. You had a genuine conversation and discovered shared interests. One friend came over to join. The mockers continued but with less intensity — your silent act of inclusion was powerful without being confrontational.

choices.label: Report the Bullying
choices.description: Go to a teacher and report the mocking. The school has anti-bullying policies — let the system handle it. It's the responsible thing to do even if it feels indirect.
choices.feedback: The teacher addressed the class about bullying next period. It helped, but Vikram still ate alone. Systems matter, but they can't replace personal connection. Sometimes compassion requires personal risk, not just procedural action.

choices.label: Stay at Your Table
choices.description: You feel bad for Vikram, but getting involved could make things awkward. He'll find his own friends eventually. Everyone goes through adjustment periods. You can't fix every problem.
choices.feedback: That night, you couldn't stop thinking about Vikram's face. Next day, he wasn't at school. He transferred a week later. You'll never know if your one action could have changed things. Inaction is also a choice — and it has consequences too.

rounds.coaching_moment: Compassion without action is just pity. Real compassion means doing something, even when it's uncomfortable.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you see someone being treated unfairly, what stops you from acting? Is that reason good enough?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

glossary_terms.definition: Consistency between your values and actions. Doing what's right even when nobody is watching. The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles.
glossary_terms.example: Returning found wallet even though you need money - your actions match your values about honesty.

glossary_terms.definition: Strength to do what's right despite fear, difficulty, or opposition. Different from physical courage - this is standing up for principles when it costs something.
glossary_terms.example: Speaking truth when classmate is falsely blamed, even though it makes you unpopular with your friends.

glossary_terms.definition: Compassion means helping people grow stronger. Enabling means doing things for people that they should do themselves. Compassion empowers, enabling creates dependence.
glossary_terms.example: Teaching friend to do homework is compassion. Doing homework for them is enabling - doesn't help them learn.

glossary_terms.definition: When two important values seem to contradict each other, requiring wisdom to balance them. Most ethical dilemmas involve conflicts between values, not right vs wrong.
glossary_terms.example: Honesty vs Loyalty: Friend asks you to lie. Both honesty and loyalty matter. Which takes priority? This is values conflict.

glossary_terms.definition: Mental and emotional calmness that comes from living according to your values. When your actions match your beliefs, you experience inner harmony and peace.
glossary_terms.example: After returning the wallet, you sleep well. After keeping it, you can't stop thinking about it. Inner peace reflects moral alignment.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: ❤️ Human Values Quest Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
